summary: Reviews the existing ways of renumbering a site, meaning changing its network addresses, for both IPv4 and IPv6, and points out operational problems with them. It also summarises proposals for new mechanisms and ends with a gap analysis of where more work is needed. It is informational, not a standard.

eli5.summary: Moving to a new house means telling everyone your new address and changing it everywhere. This paper looks at how hard it is for networks to change addresses and what tools are still missing.

subtitle: Site network renumbering is painful and error-prone; existing tools help but gaps remain.

tldr.problem: Networks need to change their IP address prefixes when changing service providers, reorganizing topology, or consolidating addresses. This is difficult because addresses are embedded in configurations, applications, firewalls, and DNS.
tldr.mechanism: Existing mechanisms include DHCP, IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, DNS updates, and service discovery. The RFC identifies operational issues with these and proposes additional tools and approaches.
tldr.outcome: Despite years of work since RFC 1900, renumbering remains expensive and error-prone. Most sites avoid it by using private addresses and NAT, which creates other problems. Better tools and procedures are needed.

today: RFC 5887 is an Informational RFC identifying gaps and challenges in network renumbering. The problem it describes remains unresolved; most large networks continue to avoid renumbering, relying instead on private addressing and NAT. The RFC recommends that all IPv6 deployments plan for renumbering from day one and deploy tools like Secure Dynamic DNS Update and DNSsec. Several address-independent approaches (SHIM6, HIP, SCTP) continue to be developed, but widespread adoption has not occurred.

sections.title: Why Networks Need to Renumber
sections.content:
RFC 1900 identified site renumbering as a problem in 1996. Fourteen years later, RFC 5887 reviews the problem again: renumbering is still difficult. A network must change its address prefix in several scenarios: when changing service providers, when adding a new provider, when a provider itself renumbers, when reorganizing site topology, or when merging or splitting networks.

Small devices and roaming users renumber constantly when they restart or move, but this document focuses on medium to large sites that must renumber as a planned or unplanned event. Site managers avoid renumbering when possible, often resorting to private addresses and Network Address Translation (NAT) instead. This strategy avoids immediate pain but creates long-term problems, including the inability to use modern routing techniques that depend on site renumbering.
sections.eli5: A network needs new addresses if it switches to a different company that provides internet service, or if it reorganizes. Big networks hate doing this because there are so many places where addresses are hidden in configuration files and programs.

sections.title: Existing Renumbering Mechanisms
sections.content:
DHCP, available for both IPv4 and IPv6, assigns addresses to hosts when they start up. A site can renumber by reconfiguring the DHCP server, though this does not automatically update DNS or applications that cache addresses.

IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) allows hosts to configure themselves by listening for Router Advertisement messages that include prefix information and lifetimes. When a router signals that a prefix is deprecated (setting its preferred lifetime to zero or a finite value), hosts know renumbering is coming and can acquire new addresses from the advertised prefix.

Router Advertisements in IPv6 include prefix lifetimes that drive the renumbering process. A site can advertise a new prefix alongside the deprecated one during a transition period.

DNS updates must synchronize with renumbering. Secure Dynamic DNS Update allows hosts to update their own A or AAAA records when they receive new addresses, though manual DNS zone file updates are common.

Service discovery using the Service Location Protocol (SLP) or multicast DNS can reduce dependency on pre-configured addresses by allowing clients to discover services dynamically.
sections.eli5: Networks have tools to help: DHCP hands out new addresses, routers can announce which prefixes are old, DNS can update automatically, and discovery protocols can help clients find services without knowing addresses.

sections.title: Operational Issues During Renumbering
sections.content:
Despite available mechanisms, renumbering introduces widespread problems. Application-layer issues are severe: many applications cache IP addresses and do not re-query DNS when addresses change. Web browsers may violate DNS TTL values with 'DNS pinning' to prevent security attacks, preventing them from using new addresses. License management systems may depend on IP addresses. Literal IP addresses appear in URLs, HTTP cookies, and application proxy configurations.

Transport-layer issues occur when TCP and UDP sessions rely on source and destination IP addresses. A renumbering event breaks active sessions. Server applications may need to restart to listen on new addresses.

Router-related issues include cached addresses in some router implementations, requiring reboot after renumbering. Configured tunnels and VPN endpoints may have static IP addresses. BGP filtering rules must be updated.

NAT, mobility, and multicast each bring distinct challenges. Mobile IP must track changes to home and care-of addresses. Multicast addresses that embed unicast addresses become invalid when prefixes change.

Management complexity dominates the practical challenge. Static addresses are embedded in configuration files, network management databases, MIB modules, firewall rules, VPN configurations, and user laptops. Updates must be synchronized, and many embedded instances are found only after the renumbering event creates a problem.
sections.eli5: Programs save IP addresses in memory and do not look them up again. Routers might need rebooting. VPNs and firewalls have address rules everywhere. Updating all these places without missing any is the real hard part.

sections.title: Security and Technical Gaps
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several security concerns related to renumbering. Firewall and access control updates must happen in two phases: adding new rules before renumbering and removing old rules after, or attackers could exploit the interval when both old and new addresses are valid. X.509 certificates with IP addresses in subject alternative names become invalid after renumbering, creating operational and security issues.

Several technical gaps inhibit smooth renumbering. Applications need address lifetimes in the socket API to know when addresses are stale. A name-based transport layer using FQDNs instead of IP addresses would benefit C and C++ applications the way Java already supports such abstraction. The IPv6 M/O flag behavior should be clearly specified to help hosts decide whether to use SLAAC or DHCP. Router configuration tools need to support Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) for stable internal addresses.

Site tools must improve: address management software must support multiple simultaneous prefixes, and operational tools must track renumbering states. Networks should use DNS names instead of IP addresses in configuration wherever possible, though some administrators deliberately use addresses for perceived security benefit.
sections.eli5: Firewalls need to be updated carefully so attackers cannot slip through. Certificates with IP addresses in them become wrong. Programs should use names instead of addresses, but they don't. Tools to manage big renumberings are not very good.

sections.title: Solutions and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC proposes several promising directions. SHIM6, Host Identity Protocol (HIP), Mobile IPv6, and SCTP all provide address-independent identifiers, allowing endpoints to change addresses while maintaining sessions. These approaches decouple locator (address) from identifier, avoiding renumbering at the upper layer.

The IETF Autoconf working group is developing address autoconfiguration for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) that may be applicable to traditional networks. NETCONF provides a protocol for centralized, secure device configuration driven by a master database. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation supports router configuration.

The most practical near-term improvements involve deployment: widespread use of Secure Dynamic DNS Update, DNSsec deployment for DNS security, multi-prefix IPv6 with ULAs, and systematic site databases with configuration derived from a master source. Beyond that, the field needs name-based networking APIs for C and C++, better router and application support for multiple addresses during transition periods, and clear operational documentation and procedures for site renumbering.
sections.eli5: New protocols can let addresses change without breaking connections. Better tools can manage databases and configurations. But most importantly, people need to plan for renumbering from day one and use names instead of addresses whenever possible.
